content.content:
1	A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is used to move glass panes, stone slabs, and similar flat panels on site by suction gripping. A suction cup is pressed against the face of the panel, air is removed from the space enclosed between the cup and the panel, and the resulting difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in that enclosed space clamps the cup to the panel so that the panel can be carried.
2	
3	A suction grip is only as good as its seal. Dust on the panel, a textured or porous surface, a nick in the sealing lip, a change in temperature, or simply the slow permeation and leakage that occurs over minutes of handling will all bleed air back into the enclosed space. As air returns, the clamping force falls. The failure is progressive and, from the point of view of the person holding the panel, silent: nothing about the feel of the tool changes until the cup lets go, at which point a heavy panel is already falling.
4	
5	Vacuum lifting equipment has therefore long been fitted with vacuum monitoring. In one known lifter for transporting loads having an adhesion surface, a suction plate assembly carries projecting annular seals defining a vacuum chamber connected to a main vacuum source, a battery-fed emergency vacuum source that can be started by an emergency switch is additionally provided, and a pressure pickup associated with the vacuum chamber is coupled with a malfunction alarm such that the alarm is turned on when a preset limit pressure is exceeded during vacuum operation [REF:US-5310232-A]. That equipment is a plate assembly with a main vacuum source and a separate emergency vacuum source; the alarm is described as a malfunction alarm tied to a preset limit pressure, and the reference does not describe the limit pressure in terms of the vacuum still needed to keep hold of the load.
6	
7	Control systems for vacuum lift equipment have also been described in which a programmable controller interprets feedback from vacuum level sensors and battery sensors and responsively provides warnings and limits or alters machine functions, including evaluating a change in measured vacuum level over time to determine a rate of vacuum level change that may be caused by a leak and outputting a warning indication when that rate exceeds a threshold rate [REF:US-10518985-B2]. Such a system is built around a controller with memory, stored records, and machine-function interlocks, and its leak warning is a response to how fast the vacuum is changing rather than to where the vacuum sits relative to the point at which the grip would fail.
8	
9	Powered suction devices in a hand-carried format are also known. An electric vacuum suction lifter has been described having a main body with a suction surface carrying first and second annular sealing units that bound a sealed space, a control unit, a vacuum pump controlled by the control unit to draw air from the sealed space, a pressure sensing unit that measures the pressure of the sealed space to generate instant pressure information, a battery unit that is charged by external power equipment and powers the control unit, pump, and pressure sensing unit, a start button, a pressure relief button, and at least one handle by which a member gripped by the device can be carried [REF:US-10625955-B2]. In that device the instant pressure information is compared with a high predetermined pressure and a low predetermined pressure: reaching the high predetermined pressure stops the pump, and falling below the low predetermined pressure restarts the pump. A warning unit is described as being operated when the detected battery power is below a predetermined battery power, and warning information relating to pressure is described as being transmitted to an external electronic device. A closely similar electric suction cup has likewise been described, in which the pressure detection unit detects the pressure between the suction cup and the component in real time and the vacuum pump automatically acts again when that pressure is lower than a second predetermined pressure [REF:CN-110630621-B].
10	
11	Hand-carried suction devices that signal something about their own state are also known. A sucker for plate glass has been described having a sucker body defining a suction hole at a suction surface, a manually operatable vacuum pump carried on the body, a sensor communicating with the suction channel that connects the suction hole at the suction surface with the suction hole in the pump, and a sound generator that is turned on through a switch closed by the sensor when the degree of vacuum sensed reaches a predetermined value [REF:US-5184858-A]. The pump in that device is worked by hand rather than electrically, and the sound is generated at a predetermined degree of vacuum which the reference does not relate to the vacuum still needed to retain the sheet.
12	
13	A portable hand grab has been described including one or more suction cups, at least one handle connected to the suction cups for gripping by hand, at least one electrical vacuum pump for at least partially evacuating the suction volume between the suction cups and the attachment surfaces, at least one vacuum sensor for detecting a vacuum level in the suction volume, and an electronic controller configured to control the pump to at least partially evacuate the suction volume when the vacuum sensor detects the vacuum level being less than a preselected minimum vacuum level, optionally together with an attach indicator that the controller activates when the vacuum sensor detects the vacuum level being greater than a preselected safe vacuum level [REF:WO-2017156581-A1]. The signal there tells the user that the vacuum is high enough to attach, and a vacuum below the preselected minimum vacuum level is answered by running the pump again rather than by telling the user that the grip is going.
14	
15	A cordless wand device for grasping objects such as silicon wafers has been described having a housing with a hollow interior, a tip attached to the housing through a hollow tube and having a perimeter region contoured to form an airtight seal against the object, a power source and a vacuum pump positioned within the housing, and light-emitting diodes of different colors which indicate to an operator whether the power source is sufficiently charged to generate sufficient suction force to safely grasp the object, that sufficiency being determined from the voltage drop across resistors connected across the power source [REF:US-5374090-A]. The sufficiency indicated in that device is determined from the voltage drop across resistors connected across the power source rather than from a measurement of the vacuum holding the object.
16	
17	A portable electric carrying suction cup structure has been described in which a handle is fixed on the upper end of the suction cup body, a vacuum pump is provided on the suction cup body, and a control unit is connected between the power supply part and the vacuum pump, so that air continues to be pumped out after the suction cup body and the material surface have reached an airtight state; the control unit is provided with a pressure gauge by which the user can know the pressure change between the suction cup body and the surface, with a light source for displaying different usage states, and with a buzzer for sending out alarm sounds according to different usage states [REF:CN-2806399-Y]. That reference attributes the avoidance of loosening and falling during movement to the continued pumping, and it describes the buzzer as sounding according to different usage states without relating any sounding condition to the vacuum at which the cup would let go of the material.
18	
19	A digital display suction cup has been described comprising a suction cup and a handle structure, the two ends of the handle structure being provided with a switch button and a pressure relief valve, the handle structure being provided with a battery and a vacuum electric pump which is connected to the suction cup through an air pipe, with an air pressure sensor and a display screen at the lower part of the battery end, a USB charging port electrically connected to the battery, and an inner side of the suction cup provided with an evacuation hole, a pressure relief hole, and a sensing through hole [REF:US-2024424646-A1]. That device monitors and maintains negative pressure in real time and shows the negative pressure value and the battery power on the display screen as numbers for the user to read.
20	
21	Multi-cup handling equipment has been described in which two or more vacuum modules are mounted on a mounting frame, each module having a cup, an electrically powered vacuum pump, a fluid circuit, a controller, and optionally a pressure sensor and a battery, with an interface through which a user selects an operational mode of the modules, and in which each module may include indicators that indicate a functional condition of the module visually or audibly [REF:WO-2022236379-A1].
22	
23	Three shortcomings persist for a person who is holding a panel in one hand. First, the response to a decaying grip in the known powered devices is to run the pump again: the device treats a falling vacuum as a housekeeping event to be corrected, and the low pressure value at which it acts is chosen with reference to the working vacuum, not with reference to how much grip is left. If the leak is larger than the pump can make up - a torn lip, a dusty or porous panel, a cracked substrate - the pump simply runs while the grip continues to decay, and the person carrying the panel is given no signal that is tied to the vacuum still needed to hold it. Second, where a signal is given, it is given on a determination made from the state of the power source, on a rate of change, on a preset limit whose relationship to the load-holding capacity of the cup is not established, as a confirmation that the vacuum is high enough to attach, or as a number on a display which the user must look at and interpret while carrying a panel. None of these delivers the one thing a person carrying a slab actually needs: notice that arrives while the cup is still holding, with grip left over to get the panel down.
24	
25	Third, the remedies that the known equipment applies to a failing grip are remedies a cordless handheld lifter does not have. A plate assembly can be provided with a battery-fed emergency vacuum source that an emergency switch starts [REF:US-5310232-A], and a controller for vacuum lift equipment can limit or alter machine functions in response to sensor feedback [REF:US-10518985-B2]. A lifter that is carried in the hand has none of those remedies available to it: the only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person holding the handle, and that person can only act if the notice arrives early enough.
26	
27	There remains a need for a cordless handheld vacuum lifter that tells the user that the grip is failing while the cup is still holding, so that the warning arrives before the load can be dropped.
28

None of these delivers the one thing a person carrying a slab actually needs: notice that arrives while the cup is still holding, with grip left over to get the panel down.

Third, the remedies that the known equipment applies to a failing grip are remedies a cordless handheld lifter does not have. A plate assembly can be provided with a battery-fed emergency vacuum source that an emergency switch starts [REF:US-5310232-A], and a controller for vacuum lift equipment can limit or alter machine functions in response to sensor feedback [REF:US-10518985-B2]. A lifter that is carried in the hand has none of those remedies available to it: the only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person holding the handle, and that person can only act if the notice arrives early enough.

There remains a need for a cordless handheld vacuum lifter that tells the user that the grip is failing while the cup is still holding, so that the warning arrives before the load can be dropped.

The nine inventor numerals (10, 12, 14, 16, 20, 22, 30, 32, 40) are used exactly as the inventor assigned them; the six drafter-added numerals (50, 100, 202, 204, 205, 206, 208) name only parts and steps the inventor described ("for glass and stone panels", handle 16, port 22, "monitors the grip vacuum", "before a load can be dropped"). Claims 1-2 track the inventor's own claims 1-2; claims 3-4, 6-7 and the method of claim 5 recast only disclosed functions; no fabrication, modality, threshold, dimension, material, rated-load, sensor-plumbing, or numeric detail was invented, and no FIG. 4 / three-vacuum-level material from the earlier drafting-agent turn survives in the current text. FIG. 2's connection lines are each annotated as standing for a disclosed relationship rather than asserting an undisclosed plumbing point. Internal consistency checks pass: figure count (3) matches figures/ (3); each figure brief's numeral list matches the Brief Description and the detailed description; every numeral in numerals.md means one thing and appears in the text; no figure contains a section line, so no section-line designation can disagree across resulting view, source-view brief, and drawing description; and no drafting note, placeholder, open question, instruction, unresolved alternative, or internal comment remains anywhere in draft/ or figures/ (the "QA MARKER ONE" text the USER asked to be removed is gone from draft/04-field.md, and the Background opens with the exact phrase the USER directed, with no reference numerals disturbed). Two minor defects remain, both confined to the one sentence that generalizes the battery relationship. Second, the same relationship is expressed in two different vocabularies - claim 3 says "creates the grip vacuum, monitors the grip vacuum, and activates the warning indicator", while the description, summary, and abstract say "grips, monitors, and warns" - so the claims and description do not use the same terms for the same relationship. findings.title: Cordless monitoring and warning are asserted as a consequence of the battery powering the pump, which the disclosure does not state
findings.where: draft/09-claims.md claim 3; draft/06-summary.md paragraph 7; draft/08-detailed-description.md paragraph 11; draft/10-abstract.md
findings.detail: Four passages tie the lifter's ability to monitor and warn without a cord causally to the single disclosed power connection. Claim 3 reads "wherein the rechargeable battery powers the electric vacuum pump, such that the cordless handheld vacuum lifter creates the grip vacuum, monitors the grip vacuum, and activates the warning indicator without a cord to an external power supply"; description paragraph 11 reads "The rechargeable battery 40 powers the electric vacuum pump 20, so that the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 grips, monitors the grip vacuum, and warns without a cord to an external power supply, including while the panel 50 is carried"; the summary and abstract repeat the "so that" form. The only affirmative inventor statement about power is a single connection: "A rechargeable battery 40 powers the electric vacuum pump 20." The disclosure never says what powers the pressure sensor 30 or the warning indicator 32, so cordless sensing and cordless warning do not follow from the recited premise. Whole-tool cordless operation is supported, but only by the separate attribute "A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is disclosed", not as a result of the battery-to-pump connection. Stating it as a consequence attributes to the inventor a functional derivation the inventor did not make.
findings.evidence: Candidate, claim 3: "wherein the rechargeable battery powers the electric vacuum pump, such that the cordless handheld vacuum lifter creates the grip vacuum, monitors the grip vacuum, and activates the warning indicator without a cord to an external power supply." Nearest inventor passages (disclosure.md line 19 and line 7, repeated verbatim at conversation.md lines 21 and 9): "A rechargeable battery 40 powers the electric vacuum pump 20." and "A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is disclosed." No inventor passage states what powers the pressure sensor or the warning indicator, and none derives cordless monitoring or warning from the battery-pump connection.
findings.fix: Replace the causal connectives with coordinate statements resting on the disclosed "cordless" attribute. In claim 3, replace "such that" with "and", so the claim reads: "3. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter of claim 1, wherein the rechargeable battery powers the electric vacuum pump, and the cordless handheld vacuum lifter creates the grip vacuum, monitors the grip vacuum, and activates the warning indicator without a cord to an external power supply." In draft/08-detailed-description.md, replace paragraph 11 with two sentences: "The rechargeable battery 40 powers the electric vacuum pump 20. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 creates the grip vacuum, monitors the grip vacuum, and activates the warning indicator 32 without a cord to an external power supply, including while the panel 50 is carried." In draft/06-summary.md, replace paragraph 7 with: "The rechargeable battery powers the electric vacuum pump. The lifter creates the grip vacuum, monitors the grip vacuum, and activates the warning indicator without a cord to an external power supply." In draft/10-abstract.md, replace "and a rechargeable battery powers the electric vacuum pump, so that the lifter grips, monitors, and warns without a cord to an external power supply" with "and a rechargeable battery powers the electric vacuum pump, the lifter creating the grip vacuum, monitoring the grip vacuum, and activating the warning indicator without a cord to an external power supply".

findings.title: The same cordless-operation relationship is expressed in two different vocabularies in the claims and in the description
findings.where: draft/09-claims.md claim 3 versus draft/06-summary.md paragraph 7, draft/08-detailed-description.md paragraph 11, and draft/10-abstract.md
findings.detail: Claim 3 names three acts using the claim terms "creates the grip vacuum", "monitors the grip vacuum", and "activates the warning indicator". The description, summary, and abstract name the identical three acts as "grips", "monitors", and "warns". "Grips" and "warns" appear nowhere else in the draft as designations for these acts, and "grips" is used without an object, so the description does not literally provide antecedent support in the claim's own vocabulary for the relationship claim 3 recites. Claims and description must use the same relationships and the same terms for them.

Candidate, description paragraph 11: "the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 grips, monitors the grip vacuum, and warns without a cord to an external power supply." Candidate, summary paragraph 7: "the lifter grips, monitors, and warns without a cord to an external power supply." Candidate, abstract: "so that the lifter grips, monitors, and warns without a cord to an external power supply." The verbs "grips" and "warns" are not used as designations for these acts anywhere else in draft/06-summary.md, draft/08-detailed-description.md, or draft/09-claims.md.
findings.fix: Conform the description, summary, and abstract to the claim vocabulary. In draft/08-detailed-description.md paragraph 11, replace "grips, monitors the grip vacuum, and warns" with "creates the grip vacuum, monitors the grip vacuum, and activates the warning indicator 32". In draft/06-summary.md paragraph 7, replace "the lifter grips, monitors, and warns" with "the lifter creates the grip vacuum, monitors the grip vacuum, and activates the warning indicator". In draft/10-abstract.md, replace "the lifter grips, monitors, and warns" with "the lifter creates the grip vacuum, monitors the grip vacuum, and activates the warning indicator". These substitutions are compatible with, and are already incorporated into, the rewrites given in the preceding finding.
